moan.e: From Middle English mone, mane, mān, (also as mene), from Old English *mān, *mǣn (“complaint; lamentation”), from Proto-West Germanic *mainu, from Proto-Germanic *mainō (“opinion; mind”). Old English *mān, *mǣn is inferred from Old English mǣnan (“to complain over; grieve; mourn”).
moan.g: A low, mournful cry of pain, sorrow or pleasure.

mob.e: From Middle English mob, short for mobile, from Latin mōbile (vulgus) (“fickle (crowd)”).
mob.g: A large or disorderly group of people; especially one bent on riotous or destructive action.
A promiscuous woman; a harlot or wench; a prostitute.

mock.e: From Middle English mokken, from Old French mocquer, moquier (“to deride, jeer”), from Middle Dutch mocken (“to mumble”) or Middle Low German mucken (“to grumble, talk with the mouth half-opened”), both from Proto-West Germanic *mokkijan, *mukkijan (“to low, bellow; mumble”), from Proto-Germanic *mukkijaną, *mūhaną (“to low, bellow, shout”).
mock.g: An imitation, usually of lesser quality.

mockery.e: From Middle English mokkery, from Anglo-Norman mokerie, mokery and Middle French mocquerie, moquerie, from moquer, moker (“to mock”) + -erie (“-ery”), perhaps from Medieval Greek μωκός (mōkós, “mocker”), perhaps from Arabic مَكْر (makr, “scheme, plot”). Equivalent to mock + -ery.
mockery.g: The action of mocking; ridicule, derision.

model.e: From Middle French modelle, from Old Italian modello, from Vulgar Latin *modellus, diminutive form of modulus (“measure, standard”), diminutive of modus (“measure”); see mode, and compare module, modulus, mould, mold.
model.g: A person who poses as a subject or visual reference for an artist.

moderately.e: From Middle English moderately, moderatelye, moderatliche, moderatly, modiratli; equivalent to moderate + -ly.

moderation.e: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French moderacion, from Latin moderātiō. By surface analysis, moderate + ion.
moderation.g: The state or quality of being moderate; avoidance of extremes.

modest.e: From Middle French modeste, from Latin modestus.
modest.g: Not bragging or boasting about oneself or one's achievements; unpretentious, humble.

modesty.e: Borrowed from Middle French modestie, from Latin modestia; equivalent to modest + -y.
modesty.g: The quality of being modest; having a limited and not overly high opinion of oneself and one's abilities.

moist.e: From Middle English moisten, moist, moiste (“to make moist or wet; to soak in liquid; to become moist or wet; to provide with moisture or water; to satisfy thirst with liquor or water, slake”), and then either: from Anglo-Norman muster (“to make moist or wet”), Middle French moistir, and Old French moistir (“to make moist or wet.
moist.g: To make (something) moist or wet; to moisten.

moisture.e: From Middle English moisture, from Old French moistour (“moisture, dampness, wetness”).
moisture.g: That which moistens or makes damp or wet; exuding fluid; liquid in small quantity.

mold.e: From Middle English molde (“mold, cast”), from Old French modle, mole, from Latin modulus, from Latin modus.
mold.g: A hollow form or matrix for shaping a fluid or plastic substance.

mold.e: From Middle English molde (“top of the head”), from Old English molda, molde, from Proto-West Germanic *moldō, from Proto-Germanic *muldô, from a Proto-Indo-European *ml̥Hdʰṓ, parallel to Sanskrit मूर्धन् (mūrdhán).
mold.g: The top or crown of the head.

molding.e: From Middle English moldynge; equivalent to mold + -ing.
molding.g: The act or process of shaping in or on a mold, or of making molds; the art or occupation of a molder.

mole.e: From Middle English mole, mool, from Old English māl (“a mole, spot, mark, blemish”), from Proto-West Germanic *mail, from Proto-Germanic *mailą (“spot, wrinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *mel-, *melw- (“dark, dirty”), from Proto-Indo-European *mey-, *my- (“to soil, sully”).
mole.g: A naevus, a pigmented, slightly raised, and sometimes hairy spot on the skin.

mole.e: From Middle English molle, molde, mole (“mole”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *mol(h), from Proto-Germanic *mulaz, *mulhaz (“mole, salamander”), from Proto-Indo-European *molg-, *molk- (“slug, salamander”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)melw- (“to grind, crush, beat”).
mole.g: Any of several small, burrowing, insectivorous mammals of the family Talpidae.

mollify.e: From Middle English mollifien, from Late Latin mollificō, from Latin mollis (“soft”). By surface analysis, Latin moll- + -ify.
mollify.g: To ease a burden, particularly to ease a worry; make less painful; to comfort.

molten.e: From Middle English molten, from Old English molten, ġemolten (“melted, molten”), from Proto-Germanic *multanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *meltaną (“to melt”).
molten.g: Melted, especially due to great heat

moment.e: From Middle English moment, from Old French moment, from Latin mōmentum.
moment.g: A particular point, or relatively small region.

momentary.e: From Middle English momentare, from Late Latin mōmentārius (“of brief duration”), from mōmentum (“a short time, an instant”). By surface analysis, moment + -ary.

monetary.e: From Middle French monétaire, from Late Latin monētārius (“pertaining to money”), from Latin monētārius (“of a mint”), from monēta (“mint, coinage”), from the presence—from 273 BC to AD 84—of the chief Roman mint at the Templum Iunonis Monetae (“Temple of Juno Moneta”), q.v.
monetary.g: Of, pertaining to, or consisting of money.

money.e: From Middle English moneye, moneie, money, borrowed from Anglo-Norman muneie (“money”), from Latin monēta (“money, a place for coining money, coin, mint”), from the name of the temple of Juno Moneta in Rome, where a mint was. In this sense, displaced native Old English feoh, whence English fee.
money.g: A generally accepted means of exchange.

moneylender.g: A person who lends money and charges interest, especially one who is not part of the official financial industry.

monitor.e: From Latin monitor (“warner”), from perfect passive participle monitus (“warning”), from verb monere (“to warn, admonish, remind”). Warship sense is from USS Monitor, the first ship of this type.
monitor.g: Someone who watches over something; a person in charge of something or someone.

monster.e: From Middle English monstre, from Old French monstre, mostre, moustre, from Latin mōnstrum.
monster.g: A terrifying and dangerous creature, especially one of an imaginary or fictional kind.

monstrous.e: From Middle English monstrous, from Old French monstrueuse, monstrüos, from Latin mōnstrōsus. By surface analysis, monster + -ous.

month.e: From Middle English mon(e)th, from Old English mōnaþ, from Proto-West Germanic *mānōþ, from Proto-Germanic *mēnōþs (“month”), from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”), probably derived from *meh₁- (“measure”) with moon-cycles being used to measure time. Eclipsed non-native Old English calend (“month”), borrowed from Latin calendae.
month.g: A period into which a year is divided, historically based on the phases of the moon.

monthly.e: From month + -ly (adjectival suffix), perhaps via Middle English *monethly (attested only adverbially), from Old English mōnaþlīċ (“monthly”), from Proto-West Germanic *mānōþlīk, from Proto-Germanic *mēnōþlīkaz (“monthly”).
From Middle English monethly, equivalent to month + -ly (adverbial suffix).

monument.e: From Middle English monument, from Old French monument, from Latin monumentum (“memorial, monument, tomb”), from monēre (“to remind”). Partially displaced Old English bēacn.
monument.g: A structure built for commemorative or symbolic reasons, or as a memorial; a commemoration.

moon.e: From Middle English mone, from Old English mōna (“moon”), from Proto-West Germanic *mānō, from Proto-Germanic *mēnô (“moon”), from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon; month”), probably from *meh₁- (“to measure”).
moon.g: Any natural satellite of a planet.

moor.e: From Middle English mor, from Old English mōr, from Proto-West Germanic *mōr, from Proto-Germanic *mōraz, from Proto-Indo-European *móri. Scots muir, Dutch moer, Old Saxon mōr, Old Saxon mūr, German Moor and perhaps also Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐍂𐌴𐌹 (marei).
moor.g: An extensive waste covered with patches of heath, and having a poor, light (and usually acidic) soil, but sometimes marshy, and abounding in

moor.e: From Middle English moren, from unattested Old English *mārian, from Proto-West Germanic *mairōn (“to moor, fasten to”), related to *maida- (“post”), from Proto-Indo-European *mēyt-, *meyt-, from *mēy-, *mey- (“stake, pole”).
moor.g: To cast anchor or become fastened.

moral.e: From Middle English moral, from Old French moral, from Latin mōrālis (“relating to manners or morals”) (first used by Cicero, to translate Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós, “moral”)), from mos (“manner, custom”).
moral.g: Of or relating to principles of right and wrong in behaviour, especially conforming to principles of rectitude.

more.e: From Middle English more, from Old English māra (“more”), from Proto-West Germanic *maiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *maizô (“more”), from Proto-Indo-European *mē- (“many”).
more.g: To a greater degree or extent.

moreover.e: From Middle English moreover, moreovere, morover, mooreover, more-overe, mare over, equivalent to more + over.
moreover.g: In addition to what has been said.

morning.e: From Middle English morwenynge, from morwen + -ynge. By surface analysis, morn + -ing.
morning.g: The early part of the day, especially from midnight to noon.

morrow.e: From Middle English morwe, apocopic form of morwen, from Old English morgen, from Proto-West Germanic *morgan, *morgin, from Proto-Germanic *murganaz, *murginaz; compare Dutch morgen and German Morgen.

morsel.e: From Middle English morsel, from Old French morsel, from Medieval Latin morsellum (“a bit, a little piece”), diminutive of Latin morsum (“a bit”), neuter of morsus, perfect passive participle of mordeo (“to bite”).
morsel.g: A small fragment or share of something, commonly applied to food.

mortal.e: From Middle English mortal, mortel, from Old French mortal, mortel, and their source Latin mortālis, from mors (“death”). In this sense, displaced native deadly, from Old English dēadlīċ.
mortal.g: Susceptible to death by aging, sickness, injury, or wound; not immortal.

mortality.e: From Old French mortalite, from Latin mortālitās, from mortālis (“relating to death”), from mors (“death”); equivalent to mortal + -ity.
mortality.g: The state or quality of being mortal.

mortally.e: From Middle English mortally, equivalent to mortal + -ly.
mortally.g: Fatally; in such a way as to cause death.

mortar.e: From Middle English morter, from Old French mortier, from Latin mortārium.
mortar.g: A mixture of lime or cement, sand and water used for bonding building blocks.

mortgage.e: From Middle English morgage and Middle French mortgage, from Anglo-Norman morgage, from Old French mort gage (“dead pledge”), after a translation of judicial Medieval Latin mortuum wadium, with wadium from Frankish *wadi (“wager, pledge”).
mortgage.g: A legal agreement in which a borrower pledges real property as collateral for a loan used to purchase or refinance that property.

mortify.e: From Anglo-Norman mortifier, Middle French mortifier, from Late Latin mortificō (“cause death”), from Latin mors (“death”) + -ficō (“-fy”).
mortify.g: To discipline (one's body, appetites etc.) by suppressing desires; to practise abstinence on.

mosaic.e: From Middle French mosaïque, from Italian mosaico, from Medieval Latin musaicum, from Late Latin musivum (opus), from Latin museum, musaeum, probably from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)).
mosaic.g: A piece of artwork created by placing colored pieces (usually tiles, either regular or irregular in shape) in a pattern so as to create a pi

most.e: From Middle English most, moste, from Old English mǣst, māst, from Proto-Germanic *maistaz, *maist.

mote.e: From Middle English mot, from Old English mot (“grain of sand; mote; atom”), from Proto-West Germanic *mot (“grain of dirt or sand, speck”). Perhaps linked to English mud.

From Middle English moten, from Old English mōtan (“to be allowed, be able to, have the opportunity to, be compelled to, may, must”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtaną (“to be able to, have to, be delegated”), from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to acquire, possess, be in charge of”).

moth.e: From Middle English moth, moththe, motthe, moght, mohþe, mouȝte, from Old English moþþe, mohþe, mohþa, from Proto-West Germanic *moþþā, from Proto-Germanic *maþô ~ *muttaz (“insect, worm, maggot”), from Proto-Indo-European *mutn-, *mut- (“worm”).
moth.g: Any flying insect of the order Lepidoptera not in the superfamily Papilionoidea, most species of which are nocturnal and can be distinguishe

moth.e: From Hindi मोठ (moṭh); see moth bean.

mother.e: From Middle English moder, from Old English mōdor, from Proto-West Germanic *mōder, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Some have proposed that the "dregs" sense is from Middle Dutch modder (“filth”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“sediment”), but modder is not known in this meaning.
mother.g: A female parent, especially of a human; a female who parents a child (which she has given birth to, adopted, fostered, etc).

mother.e: From Middle English modren, from the noun (see above).
mother.g: To give birth to or produce (as its female parent) a child. (Compare father.)

mother-in-law.e: From Middle English moder in lawe; equivalent to mother + -in-law.

mother-of-pearl.e: Calque of Latin māter perlārum, with the first element perhaps connected in popular imagination with obsolete mother (“dregs”). Possibly referring to the fact that the nacre-lined shells are the belly (“mother”) in which pearls are produced.
mother-of-pearl.g: The hard pearly inner layer of certain mollusk shells; nacre.

motion.e: From Middle English mocioun, mocion, from Anglo-Norman motion, Middle French motion, and their etymon Latin mōtiō (“movement, motion”), related to movēre, from Proto-Indo-European *m(y)ewh₁- (“to move”).
motion.g: A change whereby something goes from one place to another; a state of progression from one place to another; a change of position with respe

motive.e: From Middle English motif, from Anglo-Norman motif, Middle French motif, and their source, Late Latin motivum (“motive, moving cause”), neuter of motivus.
motive.g: An idea or communication that makes one want to act, especially from spiritual sources; a divine prompting.

mound.e: From earlier meaning "hedge, fence", from Middle English mound, mund (“protection, boundary, raised earthen rampart”), from Old English mund (“hand, hand of protection, protector, guardianship”), from Proto-West Germanic *mundu, from Proto-Germanic *mundō (“hand”), *munduz (“protection, patron”).
mound.g: An artificial hill or elevation of earth; a raised bank; an embankment thrown up for defense

mount.e: From Middle English mount, munt, from Old English munt, from Latin mōns (“a hill, mountain”), from a root seen also in ēmineō (“to project, to protrude”) (English eminent). Not related to mound.
From Middle English mounten, from Anglo-Norman munter, from Vulgar Latin *montāre (“climb”), from Latin montem (“mountain”). The noun derives from the verb.
mount.g: An animal, usually a horse, used to ride on.

mountain.e: From Middle English mountayne, mountain, montaigne, from Anglo-Norman muntaine, muntaigne, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem (“mountain”), from Proto-Indo-European *monti (compare Welsh mynydd (“mountain”), Albanian mat (“bank, shore”), Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬙𐬌 (mati, “promontory”)), from *men- (“to project, stick out”).
mountain.g: An elevation of land of considerable dimensions rising more or less abruptly, forming a conspicuous figure in the landscape, usually having

mountaintop.g: Situated or occurring on the summit of a mountain.

mourn.e: From Middle English mornen, mournen, from Old English murnan, from Proto-Germanic *murnaną.
mourn.g: To express sadness or sorrow for; to grieve over (especially a death).

mourner.e: From Middle English mourner, mornere, equivalent to mourn + -er.
mourner.g: Someone filled with or expressing grief or sadness, especially over a death; someone who mourns.

mourning.g: The act of expressing or feeling sorrow or regret; lamentation.

mouse.e: From Middle English mous, from Old English mūs, from Proto-West Germanic *mūs, from Proto-Germanic *mūs, from Proto-Indo-European *múHs.
mouse.g: Any mammal of the many rodent families (especially Muridae) that have a small body and a long tail.

mouth.e: From Middle English mouth, from Old English mūþ, from Proto-West Germanic *munþ, from Proto-Germanic *munþaz (“mouth”), from Proto-Indo-European *ment- (“to chew; jaw, mouth”).
mouth.g: The front opening of a creature through which food is ingested.

movable.e: From Old French movable. By surface analysis, move + -able.
movable.g: Capable of being moved, lifted, carried, drawn, turned, or conveyed, or in any way made to change place or posture; not fixed or stationary.

move.e: From Middle English moven, moeven, meven, borrowed from Old Northern French mover, moveir and Old French mouver, moveir (“to move”) (compare modern French mouvoir from Old French movoir), from Latin movēre (“move; change, exchange, go in or out, quit”), from Proto-Indo-European *m(y)ewh₁- (“to move, drive”). Largely displaced native English stir.
move.g: To change place or posture; to go, in any manner, from one place or position to another.

movement.e: From Middle English mevement, from Old French movement (modern French mouvement), from movoir + -ment; cf. also Medieval Latin movimentum, from Latin movere (“move”). In this sense, displaced native Old English styring, which led to Modern English stirring. Morphologically move + -ment.
movement.g: Physical motion between points in space.

mow.e: From Middle English mowen (participle mowen), from Old English māwan (past tense mēow, past participle māwen), from Proto-West Germanic *māan, from Proto-Germanic *mēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂meh₁- (“to mow, reap”).
mow.g: To cut down grass or crops.

mow.e: From Middle English mowe, from Old French moe (“grimace”), from Frankish *mauwa (“pout, protruding lip”), from Proto-Germanic *mawwō (“muff, sleeve”).
mow.g: A scornful grimace; a wry face.

mower.e: From Middle English mowere, equivalent to mow + -er.
mower.g: A lawnmower, a machine used to cut grass on lawns.

mowing.e: From Middle English mowynge; equivalent to mow + -ing.
mowing.g: The activity by which something is mown.
